source: Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 7(2))
finding: Re-fit power and exponential curves to unaveraged learning series. The exponential won in every unaveraged data set. Averaging data biased the result toward the power law. This confirms the earlier second-hand report (gap 10).
numbers: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments. Exponential fit better in 82.2% of series (range 64% to 93% across sets); 2.5% ties excluded. APEX function beat a power function with an extra pre-experiment practice parameter.
quote: The exponential function fit better than the power function in all the unaveraged data sets.
limits: Tests curve shape only, not compilation. ACT-R compilation can produce curves that are not pure power laws, so this does not refute the mechanism, only the old power-law target.
agent_relevance: Do not tune promotion rules to a power-law savings curve. Track per-item improvement, not averages over items.

source: Gianferrara, Betts & Anderson (2021) Cognitive and motor skill transfer across speeds: A video game study (PLOS ONE)
finding: Humans played Auto Orbit at one speed then another. Skill transferred only after recalibrating action timing. In the ACT-R model, proceduralisation by production compilation carried over from speed to speed, while control tuning handled the speed-specific timing. Compilation was a fixed model component and was not switched off to test it (gap 10: the critique's note stands).
numbers: 80 participants kept, 20 per transfer-speed condition (age M=30.0, SD=5.1). Speeds high vs low (low = all timings x0.5). ABA design. Utility rule U(n)=U(n-1)+a[R-U(n-1)].
quote: the proceduralization of the instructions via production compilation, which gets transferred from speed to speed.
limits: No compilation-off ablation. Transfer claim rests on model fit, in the Anderson control-tuning tradition.
agent_relevance: Split what is routine (steps, reusable) from what needs recalibrating per setting (timings, parameters). A stored routine should carry its tunable parameters apart from its steps.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
finding: Curated skills raise pass rate on average. Skills the agent writes for itself before solving lower it. A stored routine is only helpful when it is verified and from outside the failing loop (gaps 5, 7).
numbers: 87 tasks, matched no-skills vs curated arms. Mean pass rate 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 pp; range +4.1 to +25.7 pp over configurations). Self-generated skills: -8.1 pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro) vs no skills, while curated gave +18.2 to +24.8 pp on the same three.
quote: Self-generated Skills land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations
limits: Self-generated skills are written before the task, not after a verified success, so this is unlike Voyager or ACT-R compilation. Three configurations only. Numbers are from the updated version of the paper.
agent_relevance: Never write routines from the model's own unverified plan. Commit only after a verified success or from checked material.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, failure-mode and design ablations (Findings 5-6)
finding: Stored skills hurt on some tasks: a single correct pipeline with no applicability limits or fallback. Fewer, shorter skills help more (gap 5).
numbers: 13 of 87 tasks had negative deltas (worst -7.4 pp). Skills per task: 1 skill +18.0 pp, 2-3 skills +19.0 pp, 4 or more +10.1 pp. Length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp. A small model with skills (34.9%) beat larger no-skill baselines (32.7%, 29.7%).
limits: Observational splits over tasks, not randomised per task. Appendix audit read from text only; task-level data not re-analysed.
agent_relevance: Each routine needs an applicability boundary and a cheap fallback to default reasoning. Cap how many routines load at once (about 3).

source: Liu et al. (2026) How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild: Benchmarking LLM Skill Usage in Realistic Settings
finding: Skill benefit shrinks as the setting gets realistic: choosing, retrieving, then adapting skills each costs accuracy. When only general skills are retrievable, weaker models fall below no-skill baselines, so a stored routine can actively mislead (gap 5). Query-specific refinement recovers much of the loss.
numbers: SkillsBench, Claude: force-loaded curated 55.4%, agent-chosen 51.2%, with distractors 43.5%, retrieved 40.1%, no curated skills in pool 38.4% (3.0 pp above no-skill). Kimi 19.8% vs 21.8% baseline; Qwen 19.7% vs 20.5% (both below no-skill). Only 49% of Claude runs loaded all curated skills. Refinement: Claude 40.1 to 48.2; Qwen 26.7 to 30.8; Kimi 33.5 to 26.7 (worse). Terminal-Bench 2.0: Opus 4.6 57.7% to 65.5% with retrieval plus refinement. Best retrieval Recall@5 65.5%.
limits: 34k real-world skills, hand-written, not induced from experience. Number of runs per cell not checked.
agent_relevance: A cheap gate: only apply a routine if its stated conditions match the task, else ignore it. Rewrite the routine for the current task before using it.

source: Xu & Wu (2026) Skill Availability and Presentation Granularity in LLM Agents: A Controlled SkillsBench Study
finding: Having a skill matters; how abstract or step-like the wording is matters little and varies by model. This bears on gap 4: no clear sign that context-style wording beats plain steps in LLMs.
numbers: 30 tasks, 2 models, 6 skill conditions, 5 trials per cell, 1,800 rows. Skill vs none: +26.7 to +36.0 pp (GPT-5.5), +18.0 to +26.0 pp (DeepSeek V4-Flash). Low vs high abstraction: +0.7 pp (GPT-5.5), -6.7 pp (DeepSeek), both CIs cross zero. One worked example: +0.7 and +1.3 pp.
limits: Abstraction levels are not the same as Taatgen 2008's pre/post-condition vs step-list contrast. Small subset, two models, task is the unit.
agent_relevance: Do not expect big gains from lesson wording alone. Put effort into applicability checks (see d13).

source: Gao et al. (2026) SkillReducer: Optimizing LLM Agent Skills for Token Efficiency
finding: Skills carry heavy token cost and much dead content. Cutting non-actionable text kept or improved quality (less is more). Relevant to gap 9: skill cost counts in tokens per call, not just steps.
numbers: 55,315 public skills: 26.4% lack routing descriptions; over 60% of body is non-actionable. On 600 skills: 48% description and 39% body compression, +2.8% functional quality, mean retention 0.965 over five models. SkillsBench: 87/87 pass on the paired check. A 10,000-token skill costs $0.03 to $0.15 per call.
limits: Measures reading cost of skills, not the cost of writing them. Quality judged by the authors' pass criterion.
agent_relevance: Budget routines: keep the actionable core short and load details on demand. Count injection tokens in every payback calculation.

source: Authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing Large Language Models and Soar for Explainable Recommendation
finding: Closest found implementation of compile-after-impasse in an LLM agent (gap 8). On an impasse Soar queries the LLM, converts the answer to a production rule, and Soar chunking stores it. With chunking switched off, LLM calls stay high and accuracy falls toward the plain LLM baseline. Rules commit after one LLM answer, not after repeated co-firing.
numbers: Datasets ML-1M, Amazon Movies, Yelp; DeepSeek-V3 as LLM; about 500 seed rules from about 10 prompt templates. Reported relative gain 4.1% to 9.1% over the best baseline across HR and NDCG. LLM Call Frequency declines to a low plateau with chunking and stays high without (figure only, no exact value in text). The extracted Table 2 has misaligned rows, so per-cell numbers are not reliable.
limits: Recommendation, not reasoning. No seeds or tests reported. Seed-rule removal drop is in a figure. Comparison does not control tokens.
agent_relevance: Supports logging an impasse-to-rule path and measuring how often the expensive call fires over time. Direct evidence that chunking cuts calls.

source: Authors (2025) NeSyPr: Neurosymbolic Proceduralization for Efficient Embodied Reasoning
finding: An explicit ACT-inspired compile step: multi-step symbolic plans are compiled into single-step inference of a small language model via a learned procedure book. It cuts latency and tokens sharply (gap 8). It needs training, so it is not a scaffold.
numbers: PDDLGym, VirtualHome, ALFWorld. Versus BoT and large reasoning model baselines: 54.3 s and 105.8 s longer latency and 6,125.9 and 2,188.7 more tokens; abstract claims 46.7% higher success than DeepSeek-R1-Distill 70B with a 70x smaller LM, and over 90% latency cut vs BoT with +36.0% success. Ablation (Minecraft): removing procedure book C: CSR 65.2 to 47.9 (-17.3); no contrastive planning -5.3.
limits: Weights are trained, so not an inference-time scaffold. Table text garbled in extraction; used prose numbers.
agent_relevance: Shows the speed side of compilation is real when the unit is learned. For a scaffold, the analogue is a short stored routine replacing a long reasoning chain.

source: Moll et al. (2026) GRASP: Gated Regression-Aware Skill Proposer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
finding: Writing skills is not enough. Each candidate skill is admitted only if it improves a held-out probe and does not regress previously solved cases. Without the gate, skill writing is no better than no skills. Closest controlled test for gaps 1 and 3 (verify before commit; wrong-reuse regression).
numbers: MedAgentBench, gpt-oss-120b: no skills 40.6%, GRASP 88.8% (+48.2; +21.0 over best of 5 baselines at 67.8%), other models +17.2 to +40.3. Ablations: no failure grouping 84.4, no regression budget 81.8, fixes-only and append-only 80.2. No gate at K=4: 63.5; at K=1: 40.1 (equals no-skills 40.6). Matched-compute variants that spend the probe budget but ignore verdicts: 70.8% and 67.2%. Batch memory spent 439 vs 411 probe calls for 62.2% vs 88.8%. Sequential and batch memory regressed below the no-skills baseline as they accumulated.
limits: Clinical FHIR tasks. Three seeds, large SDs on OOD (up to 31.9). Matched-compute check covers probe calls only, not total tokens.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that the commit rule matters more than the write step. Use a regression check on stored routines before they become default.

source: Zhang (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
finding: Consolidating experience into abstract lessons first helps then hurts. Over-generalised and wrong entries appear. Keeping raw episodes without abstraction was competitive. Direct measured counter-evidence on gaps 2, 3 and 7 (late-run decay and wrong reuse).
numbers: Abstract: GPT-5.4 solved 19 ARC problems at 100% with no memory; after consolidating even from ground-truth solutions it failed on 54% of those problems. ScienceWorld: score peaks near step 20, declines to step 100, sometimes below no-memory. WebShop (AWM): 0.64 at 8 examples to 0.20 at 128 (no-memory 0.20). Per-model ALFWorld lines and the 5x over-generalised and 20x garbage rates for cumulative vs fresh consolidation come from the project page summary and were not re-checked in the PDF.
limits: Many results single-seed (authors say so). Consolidation is by prompting an LLM with no gate, so it is closer to naive writing than to ACT-R utility learning.
agent_relevance: Do not rewrite or merge lessons after every task. Keep raw episodes as evidence and gate abstraction explicitly.

source: Zhang (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty: episodic-only and Retain/Delete/Consolidate controls
finding: In a controlled ARC-AGI stream, agents that may choose Retain, Delete or Consolidate keep raw episodes by default and roughly double the accuracy of forced consolidation. Disabling abstraction entirely matches the free-choice regime. Abstract lessons alone fall back to the no-memory baseline.
numbers: Abstract: free choice doubles the accuracy of forced consolidation. 400-step stream, episodic buffer 50 or 100 entries. Episodic-only competitive with ACE, AWM and Dynamic Cheatsheet on WebShop, ALFWorld, AppWorld (Table 4).
limits: One synthetic stream; exact accuracy numbers not extracted from the figures.
agent_relevance: Supports a store with two tiers: raw verified cases first, a compiled routine only after repeated success.

source: Yin et al. (2026) EffectMem: Effectiveness-Driven Memory Reuse for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (Findings of EMNLP)
finding: Stores successful trajectories as contracts with a global applicability condition and per-chunk subgoal and expected postcondition. Checking applicability before reuse gives most of the gain. A condition-style format test in an LLM (gap 4), though it adds a check step and is not a pure wording test.
numbers: ScienceWorld, Qwen3-8B: baseline score 33.8, SR 15%, 44.0 steps; plus validity-gated routing 71.4, SR 51%, 30.1 steps; plus execution with correction 76.0, SR 65%, 25.9 steps. Qwen3-Max SR: ALFWorld 93.3%, ScienceWorld 82.0%, WebShop 67.2%. Qwen3-8B beats ExpeL by 41.0 / 20.0 / 14.9 points (ALFWorld / ScienceWorld / WebShop).
limits: No arm that stores the same trajectories as plain step lists with the same check. Gain mixes format, retrieval gating and runtime verification. One ablation model.
agent_relevance: Store pre- and post-conditions with each routine and check them at use time. The LLM version of Taatgen's context instructions plus a guard.

source: Tang et al. (2026) From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (MSCE)
finding: Crystallises a policy into a callable skill only when evidence-backed with positive estimated gain; skills keep applicability boundaries and reliability estimates. Turning skill crystallisation off hurts in every domain, and flat retrieval of past traces hurts more. Nearest found test of promote-on-evidence vs no promotion (gaps 1, 2).
numbers: EvoAgentBench. Flat Memory vs MSCE: Pass@1 -15.38 (IR), -16.00 (Math), -19.23 (SE); Code cost 2.0 to 5.3 turns. Removing skill crystallisation: -6.15 to -11.54 Pass@1 across domains with higher cost in every domain. Lifelong curve p0 to p100: +17.00 (Math), +15.39 (SE), +13.84 (IR); cost falls toward p100 on Math and SE.
limits: Authors' own benchmark runs; no promote-after-k-confirmations sweep; verify-once vs repeated evidence not compared. Seeds not checked. Partly conflicts with d12 (consolidation decays, see d11), probably because promotion here is gated by estimated gain.
agent_relevance: Gate promotion on measured gain and keep boundary conditions. No evidence yet for a fixed co-firing count.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: Review of 10 cognitive architectures vs 8 runtime families and 42 modern systems. Skill induction and typed compilation (GraSP) already exist in agents, but typed impasse with isolated substates and resolution compilation remains an unfilled bundle (gap 8). Most convergence is independent, not documented inheritance.
numbers: 10 architectures, 8 runtime families, 42 systems coded by evidence relation (E1-E4) and migration depth (D0-D4). No performance numbers.
limits: Review by two authors, coding is subjective; no measurements. Only the abstract and framing read in detail.
agent_relevance: Supports K20: ACT-R-style compilation from repeated co-firing is still untested in LLM agents. The open item is impasse-triggered rule writing.
